title: Balanced Tree
body:
A [[Tree]] that keeps its height near $\log n$ by rearranging itself on insert and delete,
so the $O(\log n)$ that a [[Binary Search Tree]] only *sometimes* delivers becomes a
guarantee. The definition of "balanced" varies by scheme, but it is always a bound on how
different two subtree heights are allowed to get.

The problem it solves: a plain BST fed sorted data degenerates into a [[Linked List]] and
search drops to $O(n)$. Since sorted or nearly-sorted input is extremely common, an
unbalanced BST cannot be trusted on real data.

## Rotations

Rebalancing is done with **rotations**, a local pointer rearrangement that changes the
height of a subtree without breaking the BST ordering.

```
    y            rotate right          x
   / \          ------------>         / \
  x   C                              A   y
 / \             <------------          / \
A   B            rotate left           B   C
```

Read either side: $A < x < B < y < C$ holds in both pictures, so the in-order sequence is
untouched. Only the shape changes, and it is $O(1)$ work.

## The usual schemes

| Scheme | Balance rule | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| AVL | subtree heights differ by at most 1 | strictest, so shortest trees and fastest lookups; more rotations on write |
| Red-black | no root-to-leaf path is more than twice another | looser, so fewer rotations; what most standard libraries use |
| B-tree | all leaves at the same depth, many keys per node | built for disk and databases, where a node is a block read |

All of them give $O(\log n)$ search, insert, and delete in the **worst** case, which is the
whole point.

## Against the alternatives

A [[Hash Map]] beats a balanced tree on plain lookup ($O(1)$ average against $O(\log n)$),
so if all you do is get and put by exact key, hash. A balanced tree wins when order matters:
sorted traversal, range queries, "the next key after this one", and a worst case that does
not depend on the quality of a [[Hash Function]].
